assumptions_made.assumption: Regular users are more valuable than one-time buyers because they generate more revenue
assumptions_made.explanation: Data supports this: regular users generate 31% of revenue vs. 17% for one-time buyers, despite one-time buyers being 3.3x larger in volume. However, this assumption led Alex to miss the strategic opportunity in converting one-time buyers.

assumptions_made.assumption: Revenue concentration in power users means they should be the retention priority
assumptions_made.explanation: While power users drive 52% of revenue, they already have 78% retention—the lowest-hanging fruit for improvement is one-time buyers (8% retention, 60% churn rate). Alex's logic conflates current value with improvement opportunity.

assumptions_made.assumption: The problem can be solved through marketing/campaign interventions
assumptions_made.explanation: Alex implicitly accepted the premise that win-back campaigns and onboarding improvements are the solution, without investigating whether operational issues (delivery delays, high return rates, poor CSAT) are the root cause of churn.

assumptions_made.assumption: Retention recovery requires balancing power users and regular users
assumptions_made.explanation: Alex focused on the middle tier (regular users) without fully engaging with the strategic trade-off between defending high-value power users (78% retention, 52% revenue) versus converting the massive one-time buyer cohort (60% churn rate, 1.4M users). This is a false balance that avoids the core strategic choice.

assumptions_made.assumption: Regular users represent a middle-ground opportunity between power users and one-time buyers
assumptions_made.explanation: The data supports this: regular users have 420K users, 31% of revenue, and 45% retention—a meaningful segment with room for improvement between power users (78% retention) and one-time buyers (8% retention).

assumptions_made.assumption: Revenue concentration in power users should be a primary focus
assumptions_made.explanation: Power users generate 52% of revenue with 78% retention and 43x LTV:CAC ratio. However, this assumption was not fully explored in terms of whether retention is already strong enough or if growth is the better lever.

assumptions_made.assumption: One-time buyers have low retention but are less valuable than other segments
assumptions_made.explanation: One-time buyers have only 8% retention and 3.3x LTV:CAC ratio. However, the candidate did not challenge whether converting them is economically viable given their low LTV ($62).

logical_gaps: Did not quantify the economic impact of the retention decline: what is the revenue/profit loss from the 35% → 22% drop?

Failed to distinguish between correlation and causation: did not investigate whether delivery delays (4.2 vs. 2.8 days), high return rates (12% vs. 8%), or poor CSAT (3.6 vs. 4.1) are driving churn, or if they are symptoms of deeper issues.

Did not request or analyze the timing of churn relative to customer experience events: the data shows biggest churn spike is days 14-30 post-purchase, but Alex never asked what happens during this window (delivery delays, returns processing, lack of engagement).
Missed the category mix insight: Electronics (35% of GMV) has only 15% repeat rate vs. Home & Living (48% repeat). Did not explore whether product category is a confounding variable in retention.

Did not analyze the unit economics of retention interventions: win-back campaigns cost money, but one-time buyers have LTV:CAC of only 3.3x. What is the ROI of spending to re-engage them vs. improving product/operations to prevent churn in the first place?
Did not request data on why app uninstall rate is 35% within 90 days or correlate this to churn timing.
Accepted Sam's suggestion to run 'targeted win-back campaigns' without questioning whether win-back is cost-effective or if prevention (fixing delivery/returns) is better than cure.

Did not synthesize the full customer journey: checkout abandonment (72%), slow search-to-purchase conversion (2.1%), and poor app ratings (3.8/5) suggest friction throughout the funnel, not just post-purchase retention.

Did not request or analyze delivery time data despite it being a critical operational metric (4.2 days vs. 2.8 day competitor average) that directly correlates with CSAT (3.6/5 vs. 4.1 benchmark) and return rates (12% vs. 8% prior year)
Failed to connect the 14-30 day churn spike in one-time buyers to post-purchase experience factors (delivery delays, returns, support quality)

Did not explore the product category mix as a lever—Electronics has 35% of GMV but only 15% repeat rate, while Home & Living has 48% repeat rate. No discussion of category-specific retention strategies
Ignored the app/platform performance issues: 72% checkout abandonment (7% above industry avg), 3.8s page load time (90% slower than benchmark), and declining app rating (3.8/5 from 4.2)
Did not quantify the financial impact of different retention levers or calculate ROI of proposed actions
No discussion of the personalization gap: recommendation engine is 2 years old with 1.2% conversion vs. 3.5% industry standard with ML—a clear operational improvement opportunity
Failed to address the rising CAC ($19 from $14) and declining LTV:CAC ratio (2.8 from 3.5), which suggests acquisition quality is deteriorating alongside retention
Did not request or analyze email/push notification engagement metrics (18% open rate vs. 22% benchmark, 32% opt-in declining) as a retention tool

Did not request or analyze delivery/operational data despite Jordan raising delivery times as a potential root cause. The data shows SwiftCart's 4.2-day delivery vs. competitor average of 2.8 days, and only 82% on-time delivery vs. 92% benchmark—a critical gap the candidate did not explore.

Did not connect product category mix to retention strategy. Electronics (35% of GMV) has only 15% repeat rate while Home & Living has 48% repeat rate—the candidate could have recommended category-specific retention tactics but did not.

Did not analyze the economics of converting one-time buyers. With LTV of $62 and CAC of $19, the payback is at first purchase. The candidate accepted that one-time buyers are a 'leak' without calculating whether retention efforts are ROI-positive.

Did not request or discuss post-purchase engagement programs. The data explicitly notes 'No post-purchase engagement program currently'—a major gap during the critical 14-30 day churn window, but the candidate did not identify this.

Did not explore the app quality issue. App rating dropped from 4.2 to 3.8 stars, page load time is 3.8s vs. 2.0s benchmark, and checkout abandonment is 72% vs. 65% industry average. These are likely conversion and retention killers but were not addressed.
Did not quantify the impact of the retention decline. The candidate did not calculate what the 35% → 22% drop means in absolute revenue terms or LTV impact.

Did not consider competitive positioning. ShopEase has a loyalty program generating 15% of revenue; TrendMart has strong UGC/community driving 25% of traffic. The candidate did not propose how SwiftCart should differentiate.
Did not synthesize the email/push performance issue. Email open rate is 18% vs. 22% industry average, and push opt-in is declining at 32%. These are key retention channels but were not analyzed.

summary: Alex identified that both power users and regular users matter for retention but failed to prioritize based on economic impact or root cause analysis. The recommendation to run win-back campaigns and improve onboarding lacked supporting evidence and did not address the operational issues (delivery delays, high returns, poor CSAT) that Jordan correctly identified as likely drivers of churn. Alex made no attempt to quantify the problem, analyze unit economics of interventions, or investigate why churn spiked in days 14-30 post-purchase.
